title: The Last Cellar
premise: Pest controller Ivo Amberdale is summoned to the Holloway farmhouse, where something has been leaving greasy fingerprints at ceiling height and an extra chair keeps appearing in family photographs. Digging through the cellar, he learns the Holloways' grandmother once invited a harvest spirit to punish an abusive husband—and it never left, feeding on whoever holds power in the house. As the harvest moon rises, Ivo must decide whether to destroy the entity, inherit it, or hand its covenant to someone who deserves justice; in the end he binds it not with a banishment but with a confession, naming every wrong the house has swallowed, and walks out at sunrise as the last person the cellar will ever answer to.
about_author: Orsen Sterling is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent a decade documenting other people's worst days before turning those case files into fiction. They live somewhere with poor cell reception and a very well-lit basement.

chapters.title: The Call Sheet
chapters.summary: Ivo Amberdale, meticulous pest controller and compulsive documenter, takes an after-hours call from the Holloway farmhouse: scratching overhead, greasy prints too high for any animal. His POV establishes his creed—documentation as prayer. The beat is uneasy professionalism masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Fingerprints at Ceiling Height
chapters.summary: At the farmhouse, Ivo photographs smudged handprints pressed into rafters, five-fingered but wrong-jointed. Granddaughter Mara Holloway watches him work with hollow eyes. His POV; the beat is creeping doubt as his rational framework starts to buckle against evidence that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Reviewing his photos that night, Ivo finds an old wooden chair in every frame of grandma's parlor—a chair he never saw. He returns to confirm it stands empty in the corner. His POV; the beat is vertigo, the sense of being watched by something patient.

chapters.title: Mara's Silence
chapters.summary: Mara admits the chair belonged to her grandfather, dead thirty years, and that her grandmother forbade anyone from moving it. She begs Ivo to finish quickly and leave before the moon fills out. Her POV; the beat is fear braided with guilt over what she suspects her family invited.

chapters.title: Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Following scratch trails, Ivo finds the cellar padlocked from the outside—with fresh fingerprints on the inside of the hasp. He documents everything, hands shaking. His POV; the beat is dread sharpening into obsession as documentation stops feeling like prayer and starts feeling like communion.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: In the attic, Ivo discovers Edith Holloway's journals: a 1974 ritual under the harvest moon, an invitation spoken over a beaten woman's blood, asking something below to 'sit in judgment.' His POV; the beat is horrified understanding—the pest was invited, deliberately.

chapters.title: The First Night
chapters.summary: Ivo stays past dark to keep watch. The chair scrapes across the parlor floor toward him, one inch at a time, all night. He films it until dawn. His POV; the beat is terror transmuted into grim resolve—he will see this through or die documenting it.

chapters.title: Power in the House
chapters.summary: Mara reveals her uncle Dale now runs the farm and rules the family with fists and fear, just like grandpa did. The thing in the cellar grows stronger when Dale is home. Her POV; the beat is dawning, dangerous hope—maybe the horror is also a remedy.

chapters.title: Dale
chapters.summary: Dale confronts Ivo, orders him off the property, and burns his printed photographs in the yard stove. Ivo saves only his memory card. His POV; the beat is rage and recognition—Dale is exactly the kind of man the entity was invited to judge.

chapters.title: The Covenant
chapters.summary: Reading deeper into Edith's journals, Ivo learns the terms: the entity serves whoever speaks the invitation honestly, feeding on the powerful, growing with each harvest moon until it cannot be dismissed—only passed on. His POV; the beat is cold clarity about the trap he's standing in.

chapters.title: Scratches Below
chapters.summary: The cellar door bursts open overnight. Something descends into the house proper, leaving prints up the stairwell walls. Dale barricades himself in his room; Mara and Ivo huddle in the kitchen. Alternating POV; the beat is siege panic as the house turns hostile.

chapters.title: The Photographs Change Again
chapters.summary: Ivo develops new photos: now there are two chairs, and in one frame a tall, thin figure sits between them, face turned away. Documentation has become two-way—it is photographing him back. His POV; the beat is loss of the observer's safe distance.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: A final journal page, written in failing handwriting, confesses Edith couldn't dismiss what she'd called because dismissal requires admitting she wanted her husband dead. She chose to let it stay rather than face herself. Her POV via journal; the beat is tragic complicity, justice curdling into habit.

chapters.title: Half Moon
chapters.summary: With three nights until the full harvest moon, Ivo researches the property's history: four generations of Holloway heads of household, each crueler than the last, each dying strangely after inheriting. His POV; the beat is mounting urgency—the cycle has a deadline.

chapters.title: Dale's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dale, desperate, tries to speak his own invitation to redirect the entity against Mara, whom he blames for the haunting. The cellar answers wrongly—his voice cracks, his claim is dishonest, and the scratches circle his door all night. Dale's POV; the beat is cowardice exposed, power failing its owner.

chapters.title: What Ivo Is Hiding
chapters.summary: Mara finds Ivo's own file: a sealed record of the brother he failed to protect years ago, the reason he documents everything. She realizes why he can't walk away. Her POV; the beat is intimacy forged in crisis—Ivo's invisibility was always grief.

chapters.title: Night of Almost-Full
chapters.summary: The entity manifests fully for the first time: a chair-shaped absence wearing a body of shadow and old wood grain. It spares Ivo, touches his camera gently, and drags Dale's bedroom door off its hinges—but does not enter. His POV; the beat is awful tenderness, a monster behaving like a held breath.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Ivo understands his options: destroy the house and maybe the entity, speak a false invitation like Dale, or tell the truth aloud and let the thing judge him too. Mara offers to take the covenant herself to end it. His POV; the beat is moral crucible—justice outside the law demands a price.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: The full moon crests. The house groans awake; every door opens at once. Dale flees into the fields and the shadows pour after him like spilled ink. Ivo runs for the cellar with Edith's journal. His POV; the beat is apocalyptic momentum, everything converging.

chapters.title: The Last Cellar
chapters.summary: In the cellar, surrounded by forty years of accumulated wrongs scratched into the stone, Ivo speaks the truth: his own failure, Edith's murder-wish, Dale's cruelty, the family's silence. The entity stops. Judgment requires honesty, and honesty is the only door it honors. His POV; the beat is cathartic exposure—confession as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dale survives, broken and confessed-to by the thing that hunted him; he signs the farm over to Mara and leaves. The chairs are gone from every photograph except one: Ivo's own, where a second chair waits, empty, patient. His POV; the beat is exhausted, ambiguous peace.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ivo files his final report on the Holloway job—complete, honest, unredacted—and feels the extra chair's presence recede, satisfied by truth rather than blood. He takes a new call: scratching overhead, prints too high. This time, he knows how to listen. His POV; the beat is quiet continuation—identity accepted, vigil kept.
